question.text: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function: \[ f_X(x) = \begin{cases} 4e^{-4x}, \quad& x > 0 \\[5pt] 0, \quad & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \] If $Y = 2X,$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$
question.explanation:
To compute the probability density function of a random variable $Y,$ where $Y = u(X)$ is a continuous, strictly monotonic function of a continuous random variable $X,$ we follow two steps:

  • First, we find an expression for $F_Y$ terms of $F_X,$ where $F_Y$ and $F_X$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $Y$ and $X,$ respectively.

  • Then, we differentiate $F_Y$ to get the probability density function $f_Y.$

Before we start, note that $Y = 2X$ is a strictly increasing function of $X.$ Moreover, for $x > 0,$ we have $y > 0.$

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $y > 0,$ we have

\begin{align*} F_Y(y) &= P(Y \leq y) \\[5pt] &= P\left( 2X \leq y \right) \\[5pt] &= P \left( X \leq \dfrac{y}{2} \right)\\[5pt] &=F_X\left( \dfrac{y}{2} \right). \end{align*}

To compute the PDF $f_Y(y)$ for $y > 0,$ we differentiate $F_Y$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

\begin{align*} f_Y(y) &=F'_Y(y) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac12 \cdot F'_X\left(\dfrac{y}{2}\right) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac12 \cdot f_X\left(\dfrac{y}{2}\right). \end{align*}

Applying the definition of $f_X,$ we finally arrive at \begin{align*} f_Y(y) &=\dfrac12 \cdot f_X\left(\dfrac{y}{2}\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac12 \cdot 4e^{-4\cdot y/2}\\[5pt] &=2e^{-2y}. \end{align*}

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

\begin{align*} f_Y(y) &= \begin{cases} 2e^{-2y}, &\quad y > 0 \\[5pt] 0, &\quad \textrm{otherwise.} \end{cases} \end{align*}

question.text: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function: \[ f_X(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{3}2(1-x^2), \quad& 0 < x < 1 \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases}\] If $Y =\dfrac X3,$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$
question.explanation:
To compute the probability density function of a random variable $Y,$ where $Y = u(X)$ is a continuous, strictly monotonic function of a continuous random variable $X,$ we follow two steps:

  • First, we find an expression for $F_Y$ in terms of $F_X,$ where $F_Y$ and $F_X$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $Y$ and $X,$ respectively.

  • Then, we differentiate $F_Y$ to get the probability density function $f_Y.$

Before we start, note that $Y =\dfrac X3$ is a strictly decreasing function of $X.$ Moreover, for $0 < x < 1,$ we have $0 < y < \dfrac13.$

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0 < y < \dfrac 13,$ we have

\begin{align*} F_Y(y) &= P(Y \leq y) \\[5pt] &= P\left(\dfrac X3\leq y\right) \\[5pt] &= P\left(X \leq 3y\right) \\[5pt] &=F_X\left(3y\right). \end{align*}

To compute the PDF $f_Y(y)$ for $0 < y < \dfrac 13,$ we differentiate $F_Y$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

\begin{align*} f_Y(y) &=F'_Y(y) \\[5pt] &=3\cdot F'_X\left(3y\right) \\[5pt] &=3\cdot f_X\left(3y\right). \end{align*}

Applying the definition of $f_X,$ we finally arrive at

\begin{align*} f_Y(y) &=3\cdot f_X\left(3y\right) \\[5pt] &= 3\cdot\dfrac{3}2(1-(3y)^2) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac {9}2(1-9y^2) . \end{align*}

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

\[ f_Y(y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{9}{2}(1-9y^2), &\quad 0< y < \dfrac13 \\[5pt] 0, &\quad \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases}\]

question.text: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function: \[ f_X(x) = \begin{cases} -2x, \quad& -1 \lt x \lt 0 \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \] If $Y = 10X,$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$
question.explanation:
To compute the probability density function of a random variable $Y,$ where $Y = u(X)$ is a continuous, strictly monotonic function of a continuous random variable $X,$ we follow two steps:

  • First, we find an expression for $F_Y$ terms of $F_X,$ where $F_Y$ and $F_X$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $Y$ and $X,$ respectively.

  • Then, we differentiate $F_Y$ to get the probability density function $f_Y.$

Before we start, note that $Y =10X$ is a strictly increasing function of $X.$ Moreover, for $ -1 \lt x \lt 0 ,$ we have $ -10 \lt y \lt 0 .$

Note: Image not drawn to scale.

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $-10 \lt y \lt 0,$ we have \begin{align*} F_Y(y) &= P(Y \leq y) \\[5pt] &= P\left( 10X \leq y \right) \\[5pt] &= P \left( X \leq 0.1y \right) \\[5pt] &=F_X\left(0.1y\right) \end{align*}

To compute the PDF $f_Y(y)$ for $-10 \lt y \lt 0,$ we differentiate $F_Y$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

\begin{align*} f_Y(y) &= F'_Y(y) \\[5pt] &= 0.1 \cdot F'_X(0.1y) \\[5pt] &= 0.1\cdot f_X(0.1y). \end{align*}

Applying the definition of $f_X,$ we finally arrive at \begin{align*} f_Y(y) &= 0.1 \cdot f_X(0.1y)\\[5pt] &= 0.1 \cdot (-2)\cdot 0.1y\\[5pt] &= -0.02y. \end{align*}

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

\[ f_Y(y) = \begin{cases} -0.02y, & -10 \lt y \lt 0 \\[5pt] 0, \quad& \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

question.text: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function: \[ f_X(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{2x}3, \quad&1< x < 2 \\[5pt] 0, \quad & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \] If $Y =2X,$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$
question.explanation:
To compute the probability density function of a random variable $Y,$ where $Y = u(X)$ is a continuous, strictly monotonic function of a continuous random variable $X,$ we follow two steps:

  • First, we find an expression for $F_Y$ in terms of $F_X,$ where $F_Y$ and $F_X$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $Y$ and $X,$ respectively.

  • Then, we differentiate $F_Y$ to get the probability density function $f_Y.$

Before we start, note that $Y =2X $ is a strictly increasing function of $X.$ Moreover, for $1< x < 2,$ we have $2 < y < 4.$

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $2 < y < 4,$ we have

\begin{align*} F_Y(y) &= P(Y \leq y) \\[5pt] &= P\left(2X \leq y \right) \\[5pt] &= P \left( X \leq \dfrac y{2}\right) \\[5pt] &= F_X \left(\dfrac y{2}\right) \end{align*}

To compute the PDF $f_Y(y)$ for $ 2< y < 4,$ we differentiate $F_Y$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

\begin{align*} f_Y(y) &= F'_Y(y) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 1{2} \cdot F'_X \left(\dfrac y{2}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 1{2} \cdot f_X\left(\dfrac y{2}\right). \end{align*}

Applying the definition of $f_X,$ we finally arrive at \begin{align*} f_Y(y) &= \dfrac 1{2} \cdot f_X\left(\dfrac y{2}\right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac 1{2} \cdot \dfrac{2\left(\dfrac y{2}\right)}3\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{y}{6}. \end{align*}

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

\[ f_Y(y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{y}{6}, &\quad 2< y < 4 \\[5pt] 0, &\quad \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

question.text:
Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function: \[ f_X(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{9}x^2, \quad& 0 \lt x \lt 3 \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

If $Y = 1-\dfrac{1}{3}X ,$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$
question.explanation:
To compute the probability density function of a random variable $Y,$ where $Y = u(X)$ is a continuous, strictly monotonic function of a continuous random variable $X,$ we follow two steps:

  • First, we find an expression for $F_Y$ terms of $F_X,$ where $F_Y$ and $F_X$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $Y$ and $X,$ respectively.

  • Then, we differentiate $F_Y$ to get the probability density function $f_Y.$

Before we start, note that $Y =1-\dfrac{1}{3}X$ is a strictly decreasing function of $X.$ Moreover, for $ 0 \lt x \lt 3,$ we have $0 \lt y \lt 1 .$

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0 \lt y \lt 1,$ we have \begin{align*} F_Y(y) &= P(Y \leq y) \\[5pt] &= P\left( 1-\dfrac{X}{3} \leq y \right) \\[5pt] &= P\left( -X\leq 3y-3 \right) \\[5pt] &= P \left( X \geq 3-3y \right) \\[5pt] &= 1 - P \left( X \leq 3-3y \right)\\[5pt] &= 1 - F_X\left( 3-3y \right) \end{align*}

To compute the PDF $f_Y(y)$ for $0 \lt y \lt 1,$ we differentiate $F_Y$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

\begin{align*} f_Y(y) &= F'_Y(y) \\[5pt] &= 0 - (-3) \cdot F'_X(3-3y) \\[5pt] &= 3 \cdot f_X(3-3y). \end{align*}

Applying the definition of $f_X,$ we finally arrive at \begin{align*} f_Y(y) &= 3 \cdot f_X(3-3y)\\[5pt] &= 3 \cdot \dfrac{1}{9}(3-3y)^2\\[5pt] &= 3 \left( 1- y \right)^2. \end{align*}

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

\[ f_Y(y) = \begin{cases} 3\left( 1- y \right)^2, \quad& 0 \lt y \lt 1 \\[5pt] 0, \quad& \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

question.text: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function: \[ f_X(x) = \begin{cases} 2x, \quad& 0 \lt x \lt 1 \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \] If $Y = X^4,$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$
question.explanation:
To compute the probability density function of a random variable $Y,$ where $Y = u(X)$ is a continuous, strictly monotonic function of a continuous random variable $X,$ we follow two steps:

  • First, we find an expression for $F_Y$ terms of $F_X,$ where $F_Y$ and $F_X$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $Y$ and $X,$ respectively.

  • Then, we differentiate $F_Y$ to get the probability density function $f_Y.$

Before we start, note that since the possible values of $X$ are $0 \lt x \lt 1,$ $Y = X^4$ is a strictly increasing function of $X$ when $0 \lt x \lt 1.$ Moreover, for $0 \lt x \lt 1,$ we have $ 0 \lt y \lt 1 .$

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $ 0 \lt y \lt 1,$ we have \begin{align*} F_Y(y) &= P(Y \leq y) \\[5pt] &= P\left(X^4 \leq y\right) \\[5pt] &= P\left(X \leq y^{1/4}\right)\\[5pt] &= F_X\left(y^{1/4}\right) \end{align*}

To compute the PDF $f_Y(y)$ for $0 \lt y \lt 1,$ we differentiate $F_Y$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

\begin{align*} f_Y(y) &= F'_Y(y) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4y^{3/4}} \cdot F'_X \left( y^{1/4} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4y^{3/4}} \cdot f_X \left( y^{1/4} \right). \end{align*}

Applying the definition of $f_X,$ we finally arrive at \begin{align*} f_Y(y) &= \dfrac{1}{4y^{3/4}} \cdot f_X \left( y^{1/4} \right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4y^{3/4}} \cdot 2 \left( y^{1/4} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}. \end{align*}

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

\[ f_Y(y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}, \quad& 0 \lt y \lt 1 \\[5pt] 0, \quad& \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

question.text: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function: \[ f_X(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{x^2}, \quad& x \gt 1 \\[5pt] 0, \quad & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \] If $Y = \dfrac{1}{X},$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$
question.explanation:
To compute the probability density function of a random variable $Y,$ where $Y = u(X)$ is a continuous, strictly monotonic function of a continuous random variable $X,$ we follow two steps:

  • First, we find an expression for $F_Y$ terms of $F_X,$ where $F_Y$ and $F_X$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $Y$ and $X,$ respectively.

  • Then, we differentiate $F_Y$ to get the probability density function $f_Y.$

Before we start, note that the possible values of $X$ are $x\in (1, \infty),$ and $Y = \dfrac{1}{X}$ is a strictly decreasing function of $X$ when $X \gt 1.$ Moreover, for $x \gt 1,$ we have $ 0 \lt y \lt 1 .$

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $ 0 \lt y \lt 1,$ we have \begin{align*} F_Y(y) &= P(Y \leq y) \\[5pt] &= P\left(\dfrac{1}{X} \leq y \right) \\[5pt] &= P \left( X \geq \dfrac{1}{y} \right)\\[5pt] &= 1 - F_X \left( \dfrac{1}{y} \right) \end{align*}

To compute the PDF $f_Y(y)$ for $ 0 \lt y \lt 1,$ we differentiate $F_Y$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

\begin{align*} f_Y(y) &= F'_Y(y) \\[5pt] &= 0 - \left( -\dfrac{1}{y^2} \right) \cdot F'_X \left( \dfrac{1}{y} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{y^2} \cdot f_X \left( \dfrac{1}{y} \right). \end{align*}

Applying the definition of $f_X,$ we finally arrive at \begin{align*} f_Y(y) &= \dfrac{1}{y^2} \cdot f_X \left( \dfrac{1}{y} \right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{y^2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{\left( \dfrac{1}{y} \right)^2}\\[5pt] &= 1. \end{align*}

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

\[ f_Y(y) = \begin{cases} 1, \quad& 0 \lt y \lt 1 \\[5pt] 0, \quad& \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

question.text:
Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function: \[ f_X(x) = \begin{cases} 5x^4, \quad& 0 \lt x \lt 1 \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

If $Y = 1-X^5,$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$
question.explanation:
To compute the probability density function of a random variable $Y,$ where $Y = u(X)$ is a continuous, strictly monotonic function of a continuous random variable $X,$ we follow two steps:

  • First, we find an expression for $F_Y$ terms of $F_X,$ where $F_Y$ and $F_X$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $Y$ and $X,$ respectively.

  • Then, we differentiate $F_Y$ to get the probability density function $f_Y.$

Before we start, note that $Y = 1-X^5$ is a strictly decreasing function of $X.$ Moreover, for $0 \lt x \lt 1,$ we have $ 0 \lt y \lt 1 .$

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $ 0 \lt y \lt 1,$ we have \begin{align*} F_Y(y) &= P(Y \leq y) \\[5pt] &= P\left(1-X^5 \leq y\right) \\[5pt] &= P \left( -X^5 \leq y-1 \right)\\[5pt] &= P \left( X \geq (1-y)^{1/5} \right)\\[5pt] &= 1 - F_X \left( (1-y)^{1/5} \right) \end{align*}

To compute the PDF $f_Y(y)$ for $ 0 \lt y \lt 1,$ we differentiate $F_Y$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

\begin{align*} f_Y(y) &= F'_Y(y) \\[5pt] &= 0 - \left( -\dfrac{1}{5(1-y)^{4/5}} \right) \cdot F'_X \left( (1-y)^{1/5} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{5(1-y)^{4/5}} \cdot f_X \left( (1-y)^{1/5} \right). \end{align*}

Applying the definition of $f_X,$ we finally arrive at \begin{align*} f_Y(y) &= \dfrac{1}{5(1-y)^{4/5}} \cdot f_X \left( (1-y)^{1/5} \right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{5(1-y)^{4/5}} \cdot 5 \left( (1-y)^{1/5}\right)^4\\[5pt] &= 1. \end{align*}

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

\[ f_Y(y) = \begin{cases} 1, \quad& 0 \lt y \lt 1 \\[5pt] 0, \quad& \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

question.text: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function: \[ f_X(x) = \begin{cases} 1, \quad& 0 \lt x \lt 1 \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \] If $Y = -\ln{X},$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$
question.explanation:
To compute the probability density function of a random variable $Y,$ where $Y = u(X)$ is a continuous, strictly monotonic function of a continuous random variable $X,$ we follow two steps:

  • First, we find an expression for $F_Y$ terms of $F_X,$ where $F_Y$ and $F_X$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $Y$ and $X,$ respectively.

  • Then, we differentiate $F_Y$ to get the probability density function $f_Y.$

Before we start, note that since the values of $X$ are $0 \lt x \lt 1,$ $Y = - \ln{X}$ is a strictly decreasing function of $X.$ Moreover, for $0 \lt x \lt 1,$ we have $ y \gt 0 .$

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $ y \gt 0,$ we have \begin{align*} F_Y(y) &= P(Y \leq y) \\[5pt] &= P\left(- \ln{X} \leq y\right) \\[5pt] &= P\left( \ln{X} \geq -y \right) \\[5pt] &= P\left( X \geq e^{-y} \right)\\[5pt] &= 1 - F_X \left( e^{-y}\right) \end{align*}

To compute the PDF $f_Y(y)$ for $y \gt 0,$ we differentiate $F_Y$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

\begin{align*} f_Y(y) &= F'_Y(y) \\[5pt] &= 0 - \left( - e^{-y} \right) \cdot F'_X \left( e^{-y} \right) \\[5pt] &= e^{-y} \cdot f_X \left( e^{-y} \right). \end{align*}

Applying the definition of $f_X,$ we finally arrive at \begin{align*} f_Y(y) &= e^{-y} \cdot f_X \left( e^{-y}\right)\\[5pt] &= e^{-y} \cdot 1 \\[5pt] &= e^{-y}. \end{align*}

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

\[ f_Y(y) = \begin{cases} e^{-y} \quad& y \gt 0 \\[5pt] 0 \quad& \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

question.text: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function: \[ f_X(x) = \begin{cases} 4e^{-4x}, \quad &x \gt 0 \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases}\] If $Y = -\sqrt[3]{X},$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$
question.explanation:
To compute the probability density function of a random variable $Y,$ where $Y = u(X)$ is a continuous, strictly monotonic function of a continuous random variable $X,$ we follow two steps:

  • First, we find an expression for $F_Y$ terms of $F_X,$ where $F_Y$ and $F_X$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $Y$ and $X,$ respectively.

  • Then, we differentiate $F_Y$ to get the probability density function $f_Y.$

Before we start, note that $Y = -\sqrt[3]{X}$ is a strictly decreasing function of $X.$ Moreover, for $ x \gt 0,$ we have $ y \lt 0 .$

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $ y \lt 0,$ we have \begin{align*} F_Y(y) &= P(Y \leq y) \\[5pt] &= P\left( -\sqrt[3]{X}\leq y\right) \\[5pt] &= P \left( -X \leq y^{3} \right) \\[5pt] &= P \left( X \geq -y^{3} \right) \\[5pt] &= 1 - F_X\left(-y^{3} \right) \end{align*}

To compute the PDF $f_Y(y)$ for $ y \gt 0,$ we differentiate $F_Y$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

\begin{align*} f_Y(y) &= F'_Y(y) \\[5pt] &= 0 - (-3y^2) \cdot F'_X(-y^{3} ) \\[5pt] &= 3y^2 \cdot f_X(-y^{3} ). \end{align*}

Applying the definition of $f_X,$ we finally arrive at \begin{align*} f_Y(y) &= 3y^2 \cdot f_X(-y^{3})\\[5pt] &= 3y^2 \cdot 4e^{-4(-y^{3})}\\[5pt] &= 12y^2 e^{4y^{3}}. \end{align*}

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

\[ f_Y(y) = \begin{cases} 12y^2 e^{4y^{3}}, \quad& y \lt 0 \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \]
